newsitem.title: USA: Fed close to adopting core CPI target -- source.
newsitem.headline: Fed close to adopting core CPI target -- source.

text.p: The Federal Reserve, set on achieving long-term price stability, is close to adopting a core CPI target as the basis for monetary policy, according to a Fed source.
"The Fed views that a zero-to-two-percent range on core CPI (Consumer Price Index) is price stability," the source told Reuters.
Targeting core CPI as a guideline for policy has been "informally adopted within the Fed," the source said.
Most at the Fed, the source said, do not subscribe to the opportunistic disinflation theory -- the notion that the central bank should wait for an economic downturn to drive inflation lower.
The Fed has brought the once double-digit U.S. inflation rate within reach of price stability and does not intend to give up any hard-won ground on that front, the source said.

Largely due to the aggressive 1994 preemptive tightening cycle, the Fed has brought core CPI down from 4.9 percent in 1991 -- when the expansion kicked off in the second quarter -- to 2.6 percent in the sixth year of the current cycle.
The source said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has broad support within the Federal Open Market Committee, which meets on Tuesday, to pursue a policy aimed at price stability.
Eight of the 12 Fed district banks have submitted requests for an increase in the 5.0-percent discount rate. The federal funds rate target stands at 5.25 percent.

When the Fed last moved on interest rates -- it cut the fed funds and discount rates by 25 points on January 31 -- it did so without dissent and with six Fed banks requesting a cut in the largely symbolic discount rate.
One reason for targeting CPI is the loss of usefulness of policy references such as the monetary aggregates.
Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan, a voting member of the FOMC, commented on the notion of a numerical target as a guideline for monetary policy as early as 1992.
The Fed's current view on targeting core CPI is in line with a CPI range first spelled out by New York Fed President William McDonough in a March 21 speech.

McDonough defined U.S. price stability as being in a range between 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent on CPI to allow for the upward bias believed to exist in the imperfect -- but most publicized -- measure of U.S. inflation.
According to another source, New York Fed Director of Research Frederic Mishkin and Head of the Markets Group Peter Fisher contributed to formulating that range.
The notion has since received the support of long-time FOMC members such as San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry.
A New York Fed spokesman said the bank had no comment on the notion of a numerical target for monetary policy or the impact of McDonough's views within the Fed.

The Fed is considering targeting core CPI regardless of the fate of legislation sponsored by Sen. Connie Mack that would establish price stability as the Fed's main goal and require the central bank to use a numerical target toward that goal.
The Fed's existing dual mandate is to seek both full employment and price stability.

The FOMC discussed Mack's bill at its September 26, 1995, meeting, noting members' "initial reaction was favorable in regard to the overall thrust of the bill...(that) would restructure the monetary policy requirements to permit the Congress to carry out its oversight responsibilities more effectively."
The CPI is a key issue on more than one account.
A low CPI would not only help drive U.S. long-term markets lower along with declining inflation expectations, it would also reduce government spending on a number of inflation-indexed outlays.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose just 0.1 percent in August, the latest month for which figures are available.
